BB can therefore assemble a default-config payload that cheval's pre-flight preempts with CONTEXT_TOO_LARGE (exit 7). ## Finding

``` text
head/.claude/hooks/safety/block-destructive-bash.sh:576 — Fence regression (classifier on vs. off): `_bdb_hd_scan_body` keeps a body segment only when its first word is a fence verb, so a destructive command behind a shell keyword (`if true; then rm -rf src; fi`, `for d in src; do rm -rf $d; done`, `while :; do …`, `case … ) rm -rf src;;`, `f() { rm -rf src; }; f`, `else rm …`) is dropped entirely instead of forcing a full scan. Verified: `cat > x <<'EOF'\nif true; then rm -rf src; fi\nEOF\ncat x | sh` exits 0 with the classifier on and 2 with `heredoc_classifier: false`; same for `sh -c "$(cat x)"`, `sh -c "$(< x)"`, `tee x <<'EOF'`, and the `git push --force` variant. A body line that opens a compound command or function (if/for/while/case/until/select/function/`name()`) must mark `_hd_full=1`, or the keywords must be stripped like `(`, `{` and `!` are.
head/.claude/hooks/safety/block-destructive-bash.sh:608 — `_bdb_hd_same_line_exec` misses the common "write then run" forms because `cat` is a safe reader and the execution segment never names the target: `cat x | sh`, `cat x | bash`, `sh -c "$(cat x)"` (the quoted `$(cat x)` token never equals the basename), `sh -c "$(< x)"`, `sh -c "$(head -c 999 x)"`. Any segment that names the target and feeds a pipe/substitution consumed by an interpreter must count as execution; combined with the previous finding this is what lets the body escape.
```
